name: factcheck-calibration
description: Hand-labelled claims from five generated podcast scripts, each judged against the stored paper text. Used by scripts/factcheck_eval.py to measure precision and recall of the fact-checker per severity. See docs/FACTCHECK_EVAL.md.
labelling: Labels are at clause level. Inside each script's 'coverage' windows every checkable claim is labelled (supported ones too), so a flag with no label in a window counts as a false alarm; outside the windows predictions are not scored. Verdict, scope, category and error_type are judged by reading the whole paper text; severity is derived from them by nlp_pillars.factcheck.severity.assign_severity and checked on load. Every non-supported verdict carries a verbatim paper quote or an absence note. Provenance per label: first labeller (an Opus 5.5 subagent that saw only the script and paper, never a fact-check output), then a second whole-paper read by the crewmate that built the harness, who confirmed or changed it. The research report (nlp-factcheck-research section 5.3) hand-audited the DeepSeek-VL stage ablation, the fastText 'six of eight', the AML 'no validation' claim and the fastText outside-knowledge lines; this set re-derives each from the paper text rather than copying them.

lines.116: [HOST]: DeepSeek-VL-7B surpasses most open-source models of similar size across this whole suite. On MMBench it scores 73.2, on MMBench-CN 72.8, and on SeedBench 70.4 — which is genuinely close to GPT-4V's 71.6 on the same benchmark. That's a striking result for an open model going head-to-head with a proprietary heavyweight.
lines.118: [HOST]: On MathVista, DeepSeek-VL-7B scores 36.1, which beats every open-source model they compare against, but it still trails GPT-4V's 47.8 by a wide margin. The paper attributes this gap to differences in base model size — mathematical reasoning tends to scale strongly with raw model capacity, and GPT-4V is presumably a much larger model.
lines.120: [HOST]: The 1.3 billion parameter version tells a similarly encouraging story at the small-model end. It outperforms comparably sized models — for example on MMBench it hits 64.6, compared to MobileVLM V2 2.7B's 63.2, and remember, DeepSeek-VL-1.3B is roughly half the parameter count. On MathVista, DeepSeek-VL-1.3B scores 31.1, which is genuinely comparable to some 7B-scale open-source models. That's a nice validation that the training recipe, not just raw scale, is doing real work here.
lines.138: [HOST]: We already covered the stage-one data scaling result — more data doesn't help, and can even hurt slightly. They also tested which combination of training stages matters most. Stage 1 plus 2 alone gives an average of 57.4. Stage 1 plus 3, skipping the joint pretraining, gives 61.7. But all three stages together — 1, 2, and 3 — gives the best result at 62.4. This confirms that the joint vision-language pretraining phase in stage two is genuinely adding value beyond what fine-tuning alone can provide, and that the adaptor warm-up in stage one still contributes something meaningful even though scaling it up further doesn't help.
lines.140: [HOST]: For vision encoder selection, they compared training loss curves across CLIP, SigLIP alone, SigLIP plus DINO, and SigLIP plus SAM, with stage two shortened to 8000 steps for this comparison. The SigLIP-plus-SAM combination — their final hybrid choice — significantly outperformed the alternatives on training loss, confirming that pairing a semantic encoder with a vision-only self-supervised encoder for detail is genuinely the right call, not just an arbitrary design decision.
lines.142: [HOST]: And finally, the vision-language adaptor design ablation. They compared two broad strategies: sequence concatenation, where you pool visual features along the image's width or height to keep sequence length constant before concatenating in sequence — versus embedding concatenation, where you keep the sequence length but concatenate along the feature dimension, which is what they ultimately used.
lines.144: [HOST]: The results: Token Pooling along width scored an average of 55.5, Token Pooling along height scored 54.2. On the embedding concatenation side, their chosen Hybrid MLP scored best at 55.9, ahead of Shared MLP at 55.2 and Separate MLP at 54.5. So the hybrid approach — separate initial MLPs for each encoder's features, then a shared fusion MLP — strikes the best balance between letting each encoder's features be processed on their own terms and still achieving good fusion.
lines.146: [HOST]: Stepping back, I think the through-line across all these ablations is discipline. Every architectural or training choice in this paper — the 576 token budget, the 7-to-3 ratio, the warm-up schedule, the hybrid MLP — is backed by a head-to-head comparison against a plausible alternative. That's not always the norm in papers that ship a big model release.
lines.152: [HOST]: The biggest implication, I think, is a rebalancing of priorities in how the field builds vision-language models. For a while, a lot of energy went into architectural cleverness on the fusion side, or into curating bigger instruction-tuning sets. This paper is making the case that the training strategy itself — specifically how you manage the tension between language and vision during pretraining — deserves just as much engineering attention as the architecture. The modality warm-up and the 70-30 ratio aren't flashy, but they solve a real, previously under-addressed problem: catastrophic forgetting of language skill during multimodal pretraining.

scripts.title: Deep Dive: Realistic Synthetic Financial Transactions for Anti-Money Laundering Models

lines.68: [HOST]: They checked the LI-Large dataset's rate of gather-scatter and scatter-gather pattern transactions—laundering happened about one in twenty-one thousand four hundred forty transactions. Compare that to Starnini et al.'s real data from a major Italian bank, where the equivalent rate was about one in twenty-one thousand. That's a remarkably close match.
lines.70: [HOST]: They also found that annualized transactions-per-account and payment-type distributions—cheque, credit card, ACH, and so on—roughly aligned with real US Federal Reserve statistics.
lines.72: [HOST]: Now the modeling results. Message-passing GNNs, especially PNA and GIN with edge updates, were effective at capturing laundering transactions. Gradient boosted trees combined with GFP also performed strongly.
lines.74: [HOST]: Here's the standout finding for anyone doing feature engineering: PNA performed near-par with the gradient boosted tree baselines even without any handcrafted graph features. The graph neural network essentially learned the structural patterns on its own, no manual feature engineering required.
lines.76: [HOST]: Meanwhile, the LI datasets—remember, lower illicit ratio—were consistently harder to classify than HI datasets, due to both the lower ratio of illicit transactions and the longer time span over which laundering patterns unfolded.
lines.78: [HOST]: Transfer learning worked too. Models pretrained on the easier HI datasets, then reused or fine-tuned on the harder LI datasets, achieved higher F1 scores than XGBoost models trained from scratch directly on LI data. Though for the LI-Small dataset specifically, that transfer only worked after fine-tuning—just reusing the HI model directly wasn't enough.
lines.88: [HOST]: Now, limitations. The realism validation rests on a fairly thin set of comparisons—aggregate statistics against Federal Reserve data, salary and pension data from the IRS, and one single comparison point against real Italian bank data. There's no validation of deeper structural properties like network topology against real AML data.
lines.90: [HOST]: Also, GNN results are missing entirely for the Large datasets—the ones with one hundred seventy-five to one hundred eighty million transactions—because, as the authors state, training on that scale requires significantly more compute resources. That's notable since Large is arguably the setting most relevant to real-world deployment.
lines.92: [HOST]: The authors are also refreshingly honest about something: their own generator has a stability problem. Minor parameter tweaks can sometimes yield significant changes in aggregate results, like the laundering rate itself. They flag this as a genuine open issue for a tool meant to produce standardized, reproducible benchmarks.
lines.94: [HOST]: And they're upfront that this is a "datasets and benchmarks" paper—the deeper modeling evaluation is explicitly left to a companion paper. So treat these baseline numbers as a starting point, not a final verdict on which model architecture wins.
lines.98: [HOST]: Let's bring it home. The big picture: AMLworld is a calibrated, multi-agent synthetic generator that convincingly matches several real-world statistical patterns, all without ever touching real transaction data as a seed.
lines.100: [HOST]: And its "perfect" ground truth labeling—thanks to that transitive tagging mechanism we talked about—is actually framed as an advantage over real data, where so much laundering simply goes undetected and mislabeled.

lines.4: [HOST]: It's from 2016, right when deep learning was really taking off, and these researchers at Facebook AI asked a provocative question: do we actually *need* all that computational firepower for text classification?
lines.6: [HOST]: The paper is called "Bag of Tricks for Efficient Text Classification," and the lead authors are Armand Joulin, Edouard Grave, Piotr Bojanowski, and Tomas Mikolov.
lines.8: [HOST]: Now, Mikolov's name might ring a bell—he's one of the creators of Word2Vec, so he knows a thing or two about efficient representations.
lines.10: [HOST]: Their goal? Build a text classifier that's blazingly fast but doesn't sacrifice accuracy.
lines.86: [HOST]: This architecture forces parameter sharing in a really elegant way.
lines.88: [HOST]: Words that appear in similar contexts will have similar embeddings, and those embeddings combine to produce document-level features that the classifier can learn from.
lines.90: [HOST]: It's actually very similar to the CBOW model from Word2Vec, except instead of predicting a middle word, you're predicting a label.
lines.92: [HOST]: The beauty is that this low-rank factorization—breaking one huge matrix into two smaller ones—acts as both a computational optimization *and* a form of regularization.
lines.96: [HOST]: The third trick is the hashing function for n-grams.
lines.98: [HOST]: So bag-of-words models lose all word order information, right?
lines.100: [HOST]: "Not good" versus "good" would look identical if you just count words.
lines.102: [HOST]: Adding bigrams—pairs of consecutive words—and trigrams helps capture some local context.
lines.108: [HOST]: Instead of storing an explicit dictionary of all n-grams, you use a hash function to map each n-gram to a bucket number in a fixed-size array.
lines.110: [HOST]: They use 10 million buckets for bigrams only, or 100 million buckets if they include longer n-grams.
lines.112: [HOST]: Yes, different n-grams will occasionally collide—hash to the same bucket—but in practice, these collisions act like a form of regularization.
lines.116: [HOST]: The key is that this mapping is consistent and fast, so at both training and test time, you're working with a manageable feature space.
lines.322: [HOST]: Another thing: they use this hashing trick for n-grams, which inevitably causes collisions.
lines.324: [HOST]: But there's no analysis of collision rates or how much accuracy you lose from those collisions.
lines.326: [HOST]: And while training speed is emphasized, there's no discussion of memory footprint.
lines.334: [HOST]: There's also this claim about being "on par" with deep learning that's worth scrutinizing.
lines.336: [HOST]: VDCNN actually outperforms fastText on six out of eight sentiment datasets.
lines.338: [HOST]: It's close—within a couple percentage points—but VDCNN is technically better.
lines.340: [HOST]: The authors downplay this by emphasizing speed, which is totally fair, but it's not quite accurate to say they match state-of-the-art accuracy across the board.

lines.14: [HOST]: In linguistics, especially in the generative tradition started by Noam Chomsky, we want to explain how humans produce and understand sentences. The Minimalist Program, introduced by Chomsky in 1995, proposed that all the complexity of human syntax could be reduced to incredibly simple operations. The paper notes that this program "unified more than fifty years of linguistic research."
lines.16: [HOST]: Edward Stabler took Chomsky's ideas and implemented them computationally as Minimalist Grammars—MG for short. These grammars are elegant: they build syntactic structures using only two rules, called merge and move. That's it. Just two operations to capture the full complexity of human syntax.
lines.18: [HOST]: But here's the catch. While Minimalist Grammars handle syntax beautifully, connecting that syntax to semantics—to meaning—is complex. The syntactic and semantic properties interact at different representational levels, and that makes the interface between them tricky.

lines.36: [HOST]: Architecturally, GFP has two main data structures. A transaction log, implemented as a double-ended queue sorted by timestamp, so removing outdated edges is an O of one operation. And an index — a vector of hash maps acting as an adjacency list — giving O of one edge access. Each adjacency entry also keeps a parallel edge list, because two accounts can transact more than once.
lines.38: [HOST]: On top of that graph, GFP mines two feature families. Graph-pattern-based features: fan-in, fan-out, scatter-gather, gather-scatter, simple cycles, and temporal cycles. And vertex-statistics-based features: incrementally computed sum, mean, min, max, median, variance, skew, and kurtosis — computed per account, for example on the "Amount" field.
lines.62: [HOST]: On the real-world Ethereum phishing data, with a small batch size of one hundred twenty-eight, graph features improved F1 by over twenty percent for both LightGBM and XGBoost. Crank the batch size up to infinity — effectively an offline mode — and LightGBM with GFP hit fifty-one percent F1, beating GIN plus edge-updates by ten percent and roughly matching PNA.
lines.64: [HOST]: And here's the part that really matters for production: throughput and latency. Running on sixty-four CPU threads on a Cascade Lake Intel Xeon processor, the GFP pipeline actually out-throughput'd the GNN baselines running on an NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU, especially at batch size two thousand forty-eight. That's CPU beating GPU, because the scatter-gather and cycle enumeration algorithms scale almost linearly with thread count.
lines.66: [HOST]: Latency numbers: thirty milliseconds average per batch at batch size one hundred twenty-eight, and one hundred forty-eight milliseconds at batch size two thousand forty-eight — on the AML data. That's fast enough for genuinely real-time transaction scoring.
lines.68: [HOST]: There's also an explainability angle using SHAP. For one flagged illicit transaction, the top contributing features were the count of temporal cycles of length two, and a vertex-statistics feature — the sum of money received by the destination account. That's huge for AML compliance teams, where analysts need to justify every single flag.
lines.70: [HOST]: Now, the honest caveat, because the paper states it directly: there's an accuracy-versus-latency tradeoff. Smaller batch sizes mean more real-time operation, but lower F1, because the model can't see "future" transactions yet. Batch size infinity gives the best accuracy but is effectively an offline solution. The authors say explicitly that the right configuration depends on your application's requirements — you're trading off performance for accuracy, and that's a decision you'd need to make in deployment, not something the paper resolves for you.
